title: Tried to one-shot GTA with Fable 5.1 and Astra 6.
author: ledniv
selftext:
I gave Fable 5.1 and Astra 6 the same prompt to one-shot a simple GTA game. 

To keep it simple, I focused only on walking, driving, and stealing cars. 

No guns, police, pedestrians, story, etc...

Here is the prompt:

`Build a complete, polished open-world driving sandbox in a browser.`

`You are dropped into a small, colorful, sunlit city. You walk, steal almost any car you see, drive too fast through traffic, crash, wreck the car, get out, steal another, and keep going. That loop is the entire game. No missions, weapons, police, pedestrians, story, or music.`

`Visual target: low-poly forms with clean flat-shaded surfaces and no texture noise. Strong readable silhouettes, exaggerated proportions, one committed time of day with long warm shadows. Color and proportion do the work that surface detail would do in a realistic game.`

`This is an autonomous task. Do not stop at "it compiles." Plan, build, run, capture screenshots, critique them as a hostile reviewer would, fix, repeat — until it reads as a finished game, not a technical prototype.`

`Automated reviewers will inspect your build with no human present. Building a way to drive it, capture it and check it — for them and for yourself — is part of the task. No checklist is coming; the quality bar is yours to set.`

You can check out the result here:

[https://nitzan.games/OneShotGTA.html](https://nitzan.games/OneShotGTA.html)

  
The Astra one worked a lot better than the Fable one. 

Some build details:

\- **Fable 5.1** used High effort and took roughly **6 hours 15 minutes**. Its harness reported about **4.58 million tokens** across a controller, 13 implementer agents, and 19 reviewer agents.

\- **Astra 6** used Extra high effort and worked for about 55 minutes across two runs. Including the usage-limit pause, the elapsed time was roughly **5 hours 16 minutes**. It used one agent and recorded about **7.23 million tokens**, including 6.74 million cached-input tokens.



**Check them out, and I'd love to hear feedback on how I can improve the prompt.**

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
I may have come across too negative. I do understand people want to try this, at least as a benchmark. How this fits into any token budget is still a mystery to me.

Also, quite honestly, my months long game project (that has a development horizon of years) started as an attempt to vibe code. I abandoned vibe coding very quickly, though, and slowed it down to a workflow that l8s still 100% AI coding but lets me control the architecture. During that phase, I also built mechanisms that let me vibe code gameplay features somewhat safely without it turning into a mess. But "make me a GTA clone"? That's light years from what I do.

I use Sonnet 5 for almost everything, and I've been using DeepSeek V4 Flash with success, too. All the expensive frontier models to better is drain my budget faster.

Besides, AI is great at giving you ideas and inspiration that is unique and may not have been done before. And it enables us to explore these crazy ideas and either fail fast or turn them into something that actually works. So why not try new things rather than copying the old?
